sysd-found-054.title: Certificate revocation: cancelling trust before the expiry date
sysd-found-054.text: A stolen key stays useful to an attacker until its certificate expires, unless the certificate is revoked. A certificate can be revoked before it expires, for example because its private key was compromised, and browsers check whether that has happened. With the Online Certificate Status Protocol, the browser sends the certificate's serial number to the certificate authority, which answers whether it is still valid. The authority may also publish a certificate revocation list naming revoked certificates. The CA/Browser forum no longer requires these lists, but they are still widely used. Support for sending multiple OCSP responses arrived with {{ref:sysd-found-188}}.

sysd-found-044.title: What happens when you type a URL
sysd-found-044.text: You type an address, press Enter, and a page appears. Behind that moment, the browser resolves the domain to an IP address, opens a TCP connection, sends an HTTP request and renders the server's response. It starts by reading the URL. The scheme, such as http://, tells the browser to connect using HTTP. The domain is the site's domain name, and the path names the requested resource on the server. Next the browser needs an address. It looks up the domain's IP address with a DNS lookup. Caches at the browser, the operating system, the local network and the ISP speed this up. If no cache has the address, the browser asks DNS servers for a recursive DNS lookup until the IP address is found. With the address in hand, the browser establishes a TCP connection and sends an HTTP request such as GET /phone HTTP/1.1 with a Host header. The server processes the request and sends back a response, with status code 200 for success. The browser then renders the HTML content.

sysd-found-039.title: HTTP versions from 0.9 to 3: what changed and why
sysd-found-039.text: The protocol behind every web page has been rewritten several times. HTTP has evolved through versions 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 2 and 3, each changing how requests share connections and which transport carries them. HTTP/0.9 (1991) and HTTP/1.0 (1996) are obsolete, while HTTP/1.1 (1997), version 2 (2015) and HTTP/3 (2022) are standard. One source dates HTTP/3 to 2019. HTTP/1 and its sub-versions introduced persistent connections, pipelining and headers, all built on top of TCP. HTTP/1.0 used a separate TCP connection per resource request, while HTTP/1.1 reuses one. Version 2, the subject of {{ref:sysd-found-040}}, brought multiplexing, stream prioritization, server push and HPACK compression, but still ran over TCP. It sends compressed binary headers, uses one connection per server domain instead of 2 to 8, and splits traffic into bidirectional streams that almost solve head-of-line blocking. HTTP/3 uses QUIC, which is built on UDP, so it moves away from TCP. Neither of the two newer versions obsoletes the earlier major ones.

sysd-found-040.title: HTTP/2: many requests sharing one connection
sysd-found-040.text: Loading one page used to mean opening several connections. HTTP/1.0 allowed one outstanding request per TCP connection, and pipelining in HTTP/1.1 only partly helped. HTTP/2 is a revision of HTTP that maps HTTP semantics onto binary frames multiplexed over one connection. It needs one connection per server domain instead of 2 to 8. Messages are encoded in binary and split into frames. Each request and response exchange gets its own stream, and frames from many streams are interleaved and reassembled on the other side. HTTP fields are repetitive and verbose, so HTTP/2 compresses them with HPACK, which saves bandwidth. Two features proved awkward. The priority signaling of RFC 7540 was complex and unevenly implemented, so RFC 9113 deprecates it. Server push, an optional mode, lets a server speculatively send data the client will probably need. It is hard to use well, because the server must predict requests. Over TLS the protocol is negotiated with the ALPN extension under the identifier h2, and implementations must use TLS 1.2 or higher. It does not address TCP head-of-line blocking.

sysd-found-041.title: HTTP/3 and QUIC: leaving TCP behind
sysd-found-041.text: HTTP/3 is the third major version of HTTP, specified in RFC 9114, and it runs over QUIC instead of over TCP. QUIC (RFC 9000) is a multiplexed transport built on UDP that provides reliability and does congestion control in user space. HTTP/3 keeps the semantics of earlier versions, with the same request methods, status codes and message fields. The differences lie in how they are encoded and mapped to the transport. The reason for the move is head-of-line blocking. TCP cannot see the parallel streams of HTTP/2, so one lost packet stalls every transaction. QUIC's native multiplexing makes a lost packet affect only the streams that lost data. HTTP/3 also compresses headers with QPACK instead of HPACK, which sends table updates on separate unidirectional streams to reduce head-of-line blocking among streams. In real-world use it loads faster than earlier versions, in some cases over four times faster than HTTP/1.1, though one source says over three times. As of July 2026, more than 95% of major web browsers in use and 40% of the top 10 million websites support it.

sysd-found-182.title: HTTP/2 streams: how one connection carries many conversations
sysd-found-182.text: One slow response should not freeze a whole page. That is the job of the stream. An HTTP/2 stream is an independent, bidirectional sequence of frames within one connection, and giving each request and response its own stream is how HTTP/2 multiplexes requests. One connection can hold many concurrently open streams, with either endpoint interleaving frames from different streams. Streams are largely independent, so a stalled request or response does not stop progress on the others, although TCP head-of-line blocking is not addressed. The basic unit is the frame, with a fixed 9-octet header, and HEADERS and DATA frames carry requests and responses. Stream identifiers are 31-bit integers. Clients use odd numbers and servers even, each new one must exceed all earlier ones from that endpoint, and none is reused. A long-lived connection can therefore run out, and then a client opens a new connection while a server sends a GOAWAY frame to force it to. SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS limits the streams a peer may open. It is initially unlimited, and a value no smaller than 100 is recommended.

sysd-found-170.title: HTTP pipelining: sending requests without waiting
sysd-found-170.text: Pipelining dramatically improves page load times, especially on high-latency links such as satellite connections. HTTP pipelining is a feature of HTTP/1.1 that lets a client send several requests over one TCP connection without waiting for the matching responses. The server must answer in the order requests arrived, so the connection stays first-in-first-out and head-of-line blocking can occur. GET and HEAD requests can always be pipelined, while a POST should not be. Many legacy servers and especially proxies handle it badly, even mixing up the order of responses, so browsers disabled or removed it. HTTP/2 multiplexing superseded it, and in HTTP/3 QUIC does the multiplexing.

sysd-found-177.title: Certificate validation levels: what the issuer actually checked
sysd-found-177.text: Not every certificate proves the same thing. Validation levels describe how much a certificate authority checks before issuing one: domain control only, organization identity, or extended legal identity. A domain-validated certificate proves control of a domain name, not who the applicant is. An organization-validated one also needs the organization's existence as a legal entity, and an Extended Validation certificate needs manual human checks of legal identity. EV does not fully fix the weakness of domain validation, because an attacker could still get a domain-validated certificate for the victim domain. Until 2019 major browsers showed the legal identity for EV certificates.

sysd-found-172.title: Non-standard HTTP status codes: 499, 522 and friends
sysd-found-172.text: Servers use status codes that no standard defines. IETF-defined codes are documented in RFCs and maintained by IANA, while other values come from various servers. Among web servers, {{ref:sysd-blocks-190}} expands the 4xx space: 444 closes the connection with no response, and 499 reports a client that closed the request early. Cloudflare's proxy expands 5xx to signal origin problems, with 521 for refused connections and 522 for a timed-out contact. Some HTTP proxies informally use 598 for a network read timeout and 599 for a network connect timeout behind the proxy.

sysd-found-076.title: HTTP extensibility: growing without a new version
sysd-found-076.text: HTTP can gain new abilities without a new protocol version. It has generic extension points, such as methods, status codes, header fields, HTTP authentication schemes and cache directives. Because the semantics of HTTP are not versioned, these points persist and mean the same in every version. Version-specific extension points, such as transfer codings in HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 frame types, cannot override a version-independent mechanism unless that element allows it, as CONNECT does. New methods and status codes should be registered in the IANA HTTP Method and Status Code registries.

sysd-found-171.title: Informational 1xx codes: interim responses before the real one
sysd-found-171.text: Not every response is the last one. A 1xx status code is an interim response that reports connection status or request progress before the final response. It ends with the header section and has no content. 100 (Continue) says the initial part of a request was received and not rejected. A client that sends Expect: 100-continue and waits wastes no upload when the headers get the request rejected. 101 (Switching Protocols) answers an Upgrade request by naming the protocol now in effect, such as a newer HTTP version. 103 (Early Hints) returns some response headers before the final message. 102 (Processing), a WebDAV code, is deprecated.

sysd-found-061.title: Resources and representations: what HTTP really transfers
sysd-found-061.text: A resource can be anything, even the current weather. A resource is the target of an HTTP request. A representation is information reflecting the past, current or desired state of a resource in a format the protocol can carry. HTTP gives clients a uniform interface to a resource, whatever its type or implementation, by sending messages that manipulate or transfer representations. Because it communicates a representation and not the resource itself, implementation details stay hidden. One resource can have several representations, and an algorithm, usually {{ref:sysd-found-064}}, picks the selected one.

sysd-found-066.title: Content-Type, Content-Encoding and Content-Length
sysd-found-066.text: Every body needs a label saying what it is. Representation metadata describes the content of a message: Content-Type gives its media type, Content-Encoding the codings applied, such as compression, and Content-Length its size in octets. The media type defines both the data format and how the recipient should process it after any content codings are decoded. Content-Encoding exists mainly so data can be compressed without losing its media type,. When the length is unknown in advance, Content-Length is omitted. A client that takes a close as the end then cannot tell a premature close from a complete response, so chunked transfer encoding streams content reliably instead.

sysd-found-064.title: Content negotiation: one URL, several versions
sysd-found-064.text: One address can serve the same thing in different formats, languages or encodings. Content negotiation is how HTTP chooses among several representations of a resource to fit what a client can handle or prefers. In proactive negotiation, the server picks from the client's stated preferences. In reactive negotiation, the server lists options and the client chooses. In request content negotiation, the client uses the server's stated preferences. Proactive negotiation uses Accept, Accept-Charset, Accept-Encoding and Accept-Language headers, and the server also weighs hints such as the client's network address or User-Agent. It can save a round trip. But the server cannot know what is best for each user. Describing capabilities in every request is inefficient and a privacy risk, and it limits reuse of responses by shared caches. Reactive negotiation often works from a list in a 300 (Multiple Choices) or 406 (Not Acceptable) response, and it costs a second request. A q parameter weights each preference from 0 to 1, and the default is 1.

sysd-found-070.title: Success codes: 200, 201, 202, 204 and 206
sysd-found-070.text: The 2xx class says the client's request was successfully received, understood and accepted. 200 (OK) means the request succeeded. 201 (Created) means one or more new resources were created, and the primary one is identified by the Location header or, if absent, by the target URI. 202 (Accepted) means the request was accepted for processing but not completed, and it may never be acted on. HTTP has no way to send the final status of an asynchronous operation later. 204 (No Content) means the request succeeded with nothing more to send, and 206 (Partial Content) means a range request is being fulfilled.

sysd-found-187.title: HTTP/2 connection management: one long-lived connection per host
sysd-found-187.text: HTTP/2 uses one long-lived, persistent connection per host and port, reused across requests and shut down gracefully with a GOAWAY frame. Clients should not open more than one per host and port, except to replace one near exhausting stream identifiers, needing fresh TLS keys or failed. Before closing, an endpoint should send GOAWAY naming the highest stream that might have been processed. Requests on higher streams, or on a stream reset with REFUSED_STREAM, were unprocessed and are safe to retry. Idle connections can silently break because middleboxes discard connection bindings, so a client can send a PING frame to test one without sending a request.

sysd-found-183.title: HTTP/2 flow control: the receiver sets the pace
sysd-found-183.text: Streams contend for one TCP connection, and contention can block them. HTTP/2 flow control is a credit-based scheme, driven by the receiver, that keeps multiplexed streams on one connection from destructively interfering with each other. It applies to individual streams and to the connection as a whole, through WINDOW_UPDATE frames. Receivers advertise how many octets they will accept. The initial window is 65,535 octets for each new stream and for the connection, and only DATA frames count against it. Flow control works hop by hop, not end to end, and protects resource-constrained endpoints such as a proxy with a slow upstream and fast downstream.

sysd-found-184.title: HTTP/2 header compression: HPACK and shared state
sysd-found-184.text: Headers repeat themselves, request after request. HTTP/2 compresses each set of header fields into a field block (HPACK) using state shared across the connection. Repetitive fields quickly fill the initial TCP congestion window, so compressing them lets many requests fit into one packet. Compression is stateful: each endpoint keeps an encoder and decoder context with a dynamic table, whose maximum size the decoder sets, starting at 4,096 bytes. A receiver must decompress field blocks even when discarding the frames, because they change compression state. The Cookie header may be split into separate fields, because updating one pair would otherwise invalidate the stored field line and hurt compression.

sysd-found-185.title: HTTP/2 server push: answering before the question
sysd-found-185.text: Why wait to be asked? HTTP/2 server push lets a server send responses, with the promised requests that go with them, to a client before the client asks. The server synthesizes a request, sends it as a PUSH_PROMISE frame, and then answers it on a separate server-initiated stream. The aim is to remove a round trip: a request for HTML is often followed by requests for the stylesheets and scripts it references. In practice push is hard to use well, because the server must predict requests despite caches, content negotiation and user behavior, and wrong guesses waste bandwidth. Promised requests must be safe and cacheable.

sysd-found-075.title: Keeping sensitive data out of URLs
sysd-found-075.text: URIs are meant to be shared, not secured, so sensitive or personally identifiable information should not be placed in them. Many servers, proxies and user agents log or display them where third parties can see them. A GET form builds a URI from user input, so POST is often preferred for sensitive fields because it sends them in the content. That hinders reuse by caches, though, and uses an unsafe method for what would be a safe request. The Referer header can reveal a user's recent browsing history and any personal data in the referring URI.

sysd-found-063.title: POST versus PUT: who decides where the data lives
sysd-found-063.text: Same payload, different promise. The fundamental difference is intent: the target of a POST handles the representation by the resource's own semantics, whereas a PUT replaces the state of the target resource. Hence the intent of PUT is idempotent and visible to intermediaries, though only the origin server knows the exact effect. A proper PUT presumes the client knows which resource it wants. A service that selects the URI itself after receiving a state-changing request should use POST instead. A successful PUT returns 201 (Created) if it created the resource and 200 (OK) or 204 (No Content) if it modified an existing one.

sysd-found-065.title: The Vary header: telling caches what a response depended on
sysd-found-065.text: A server that picks your language needs to tell caches it did. The Vary response header names the request fields, beyond method and URI, that may have influenced which content the origin server chose. Its value is a list of selecting header field names, such as accept-encoding and accept-language, or the wildcard *. A cache may reuse a response with Vary only for a later request with the same values in the listed fields, so Vary expands the cache key. A * signals that other aspects of the request, even outside the message, played a role. A cache then cannot judge reuse without asking the origin.

sysd-found-082.title: The Cache-Control header: one line steering every cache
sysd-found-082.text: One header steers the caches along the way. The Cache-Control header lists directives that control caches along the request and response chain. Directives are unidirectional: one in a request does not imply the same directive in the response. A proxy must pass them through in forwarded messages, whether or not it implements a cache. No directive can target a specific cache. Request directives are advisory, which caches may implement but need not, while a cache must obey the response directives. Cache-Control takes precedence over the older Expires header, which is ignored when max-age or, for a shared cache, s-maxage is present.

sysd-found-084.title: Cache-Control request directives: what a client may ask of a cache
sysd-found-084.text: A client can ask a cache for fresher or staler answers, but it can only ask. Request directives are advisory, and caches need not honor them. A max-age directive asks for a response no older than the given seconds. A max-stale directive accepts a response past its freshness lifetime. A no-cache directive asks that a stored response not be used without successful validation at the origin. A no-store directive says a cache must not store any part of the request or its response. With only-if-cached the client wants a stored response only, and a cache that honors it answers with one or with 504 (Gateway Timeout).

sysd-found-085.title: Shared and private HTTP caches: whose copy is it
sysd-found-085.text: Some caches serve many people, and some serve one. A shared cache stores responses for reuse by more than one user and usually sits in an intermediary. A private cache is dedicated to one user, often inside a user agent. The private response directive stops a shared cache from storing a response meant for one user, but a private cache may store it. A shared cache needs extra permission to reuse a response to a request that carried credentials, and s-maxage applies only to shared caches. Private caches can be used to reconstruct their one user's activity.

sysd-found-086.title: HTTP cache security risks: poisoning, timing and leaks
sysd-found-086.text: Caches add an attack surface, because their contents persist after a request ends, so an attack on a cache can reveal or alter information long afterwards. In cache poisoning an attacker inserts a malicious response into a cache, which is especially effective when a shared cache distributes it to many clients. Cache timing leaks which resources were previously requested, since a fast load shows a site was visited. Adding the referring site to the cache key, called double keying, mitigates it. Deployment flaws can cache sensitive information, such as credentials, and a cacheable response with Set-Cookie can be reused for later requests.
